say: A supply chain attack does not need you to write bad code. It only needs you to install something. This checks two places that go wrong: the manifest listing your dependencies, and the source of a package itself.
Two things are wrong here and neither is obvious at a glance. One dependency is spelt lodahs rather than lodash. And there is a postinstall script that pipes a remote file straight into a shell.
Both are caught, with the evidence quoted rather than summarised. The install script is shown in full, because that is the thing you actually need to read.

The typosquat is found by edit distance against a curated list of well known packages. Lodahs is two edits from lodash — the last two letters swapped. That list is not exhaustive and the tool says so, because a curated list pretending to be complete is worse than one that admits its limits.
Now the other half: the source of a package, rather than the list of them.

Six independent signal sets, each reported with a line number and the snippet that triggered it. A hardcoded AWS key, masked rather than reprinted. A SQL query built by interpolation instead of parameters. Pickle loading untrusted bytes.

And the obfuscation tell: a string literal with unusually high entropy, measured in bits per character. That is what a base64 encoded payload looks like from the outside, without needing to know what it decodes to.

This is pattern matching, not signature comparison, so it can flag a package nobody has seen before. It is also why it cannot promise a verdict. Every finding is a reason to go and read the line it points at.
